summary: Describes an enhanced form of compressed RTP for links with high delay, packet loss, and reordering. It builds on the IP/UDP/RTP header compression in RFC 2508, which copes poorly with loss on such links because context gets corrupted. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Voice packets carry long repeated headers, and shortening them saves room. The old shortening trick falls apart when packets get lost. This memo makes it more tolerant.

questions: rtp header compression on lossy links

subtitle: Making RTP header compression survive links that lose, reorder and delay packets.

tldr.problem: CRTP (RFC 2508) squeezes IP/UDP/RTP headers to 2-4 bytes, but it was built for reliable, short-delay links. On links with loss, reordering and long delay, one lost update corrupts the shared context and many packets are discarded before it is repaired.
tldr.mechanism: The compressor repeats every context update in N+1 consecutive packets, and the COMPRESSED_UDP packet is extended so it can carry absolute values as well as deltas. An optional headers checksum lets the decompressor verify results when the UDP checksum is absent.
tldr.outcome: With these extensions CRTP keeps its context in sync as long as no more than N adjacent packets are lost, at the cost of some extra overhead. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: HDRCKSUM covers
facts.value: first 12 bytes of UDP data plus CSRC list

today: RFC 3545 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 2508, and the RFC itself says ROHC (RFC 3095) may be preferred where compression efficiency is the main goal.

sections.title: Why CRTP Needs Help on Lossy Links
sections.content:
CRTP, defined in RFC 2508, compresses the IP, UDP and RTP headers of a packet to 2-4 bytes most of the time. It was designed for reliable point to point links with short delays, and it does not cope well with a high rate of packet loss, reordering and long delays.

The RFC gives two example links. One is a PPP session tunneled over an IP-level protocol such as L2TP, where packets can be lost and reordered and a longer tunnel means a longer round trip time. The other is an access network built on ATM or Frame Relay virtual circuits, which do not reorder packets but may span long distances and may drop more packets under congestion than a serial link would.

The fix is to repeat context updates and to allow absolute (uncompressed) values for selected fields as well as delta values. The extra overhead is real, but the RFC says overall compression is still substantial.

The RFC also mentions Robust Header Compression (ROHC, RFC 3095), which it expects to be preferred where compression efficiency matters most. ROHC assumes compressed packets are not misordered, though. The RFC argues that enhanced CRTP can be the better choice where CRTP is already implemented or where simplicity matters more.
sections.eli5: Shortening headers works great on a calm road. On a bumpy road where packages get lost and arrive late, the old way breaks, so this memo makes it tougher.

sections.title: How Contexts Work and How They Break
sections.content:
For each compressed RTP stream, the compressor and decompressor share a context. It holds the full IP/UDP/RTP headers, a few first order differential (delta) values, a link sequence number, a generation number and a delta encoding table. A FULL_HEADER packet always starts a session and sets the full headers. Later COMPRESSED_RTP packets can update the delta values.

If the two copies of the context drift apart, the decompressor cannot rebuild headers correctly. It then invalidates the context and sends a CONTEXT_STATE packet to ask for repair. While the context is bad it discards every packet for that stream. Because repair needs feedback, it takes at least one round trip, so on a long-delay link many packets are lost before the context is fixed.

Contexts break when a packet carrying an update is lost. For example, with silence suppression the RTP timestamp jumps by a large value when speech resumes, so an update must be sent. If that packet is lost, the decompressor fails on the next packet. A lost absolute value (such as the full RTP timestamp or payload type) can be repeated in the next packet, but a lost delta update cannot be recovered that way, since a delta is relative to the lost packet. That is why absolute updates are useful.
sections.eli5: Two people keep the same scorecard. If one score update is lost, their cards disagree and every later score is wrong until they sort it out, which takes a while if they are far apart.

sections.title: The Extended COMPRESSED_UDP Packet
sections.content:
RFC 2508 already lets a decompressor guess at lost packets with the "twice" algorithm: it adds the delta values to the previous context twice (or more) and checks the result with the UDP checksum. This only works if the context stays in sync, which means both the absolute value and the delta must be communicated reliably when a delta changes. Repeating the update in several successive packets gives enough reliability in many environments.

Three changes to COMPRESSED_UDP make this possible:

  • The T bit may now be nonzero, so the delta RTP timestamp can be sent explicitly instead of being reset to zero.
  • A second flags byte is added, signalled by a new F flag, so individual absolute RTP fields can be sent without carrying the whole RTP header. The old delta flags are renamed dS, dT and dI, and the absolute flags are S, T, I, plus M (marker), P (payload type) and C (CSRC count). When C=1 another byte carries the 4-bit CC field.
  • A new I flag carries the absolute IPv4 ID, replacing the dS flag, which is not needed because the delta RTP sequence number always stays 1. IPv6 has no IP ID, so I and dI are always 0 there.

With F=0 the packet carries the full RTP header as before, and if dT=0 the decompressor sets deltaT to 0. With F=1 only the selected fields are carried, and in contrast to RFC 2508, if dT=0 the decompressor KEEPS the current deltaT. Bits marked 0 in the second flags byte and the CC byte SHOULD be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

Two usage tips are given. The compressor should periodically refresh the decompressor, which F=0 with I=1, dI=1, dT=1 does for all context parameters. And if deltas change often, the compressor MAY send only absolute values and never deltas, using F=1 with S, T or I as needed.
sections.eli5: The short message gets an extra row of tick boxes so the sender can say exactly which pieces it is updating, and it can give the real number instead of just "one more than before".

sections.title: The Headers Checksum
sections.content:
The twice algorithm is checked against the UDP checksum. Many RTP streams send a UDP checksum of zero, which means nothing is there to check. To cover that case, the compressor MAY replace the null UDP checksum with a 16-bit headers checksum (HDRCKSUM) that the decompressor removes after validating. It is never used with IPv6, because a null UDP checksum is not allowed there.

A new C flag in the FULL_HEADER packet says that every COMPRESSED_UDP and COMPRESSED_RTP packet in that context carries HDRCKSUM. The compressor MAY set it when the original UDP checksum was zero, and then the FULL_HEADER packet MUST also carry the checksum. If a packet later arrives with a UDP checksum present, a new FULL_HEADER MUST be sent with the flag cleared.

HDRCKSUM is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the pseudo-IP header, the UDP header, the first 12 bytes of the UDP data (the fixed part of the RTP header) and the CSRC list. The rest of the RTP header and the RTP data are not covered. The decompressor MUST zero out the UDP checksum field in the packets it rebuilds. For a non-RTP context with fewer than 12 data bytes, it covers what is present, and an odd length gets a zero padding byte that is not transmitted.

Because the RTP data is not covered, errors there go unnoticed on a link that does not check for errors. Over such links the compressor SHOULD add HDRCKSUM if no UDP checksum is present, and the decompressor SHOULD validate each rebuilt packet so the headers are at least correct. That can suit applications that tolerate errors in the RTP data.
sections.eli5: When there is no built-in way to check the label on a package, the sender adds a small check number for the label only. The receiver checks the label, then peels the check number off.

sections.title: Robust Operation with N+1 Repeats
sections.content:
Robustness is built around a number N describing link quality: the probability of more than N adjacent packets being lost is small. For every change to a full or delta value, the compressor includes the change in N+1 consecutive packets. If at least one arrives, both the full and delta values are updated, and as long as fewer than N+1 adjacent packets are lost, the twice algorithm restores the context.

The link sequence number cycles in 16 packets, so a gap may be ambiguous. If the previous number was 5 and the current one is 4, either 15 packets were lost or packet 5 simply arrived before packet 4. If some reading gives a gap smaller than N+1, the decompressor may apply the twice algorithm that many times and verify with the UDP checksum or HDRCKSUM.

When more than N packets are lost, the IPv4 ID is not covered by the checksum, so recovery cannot validate it. For IPv4 the decompressor SHOULD NOT try the twice algorithm and SHOULD invalidate the context and send CONTEXT_STATE. For IPv6 it MAY always try.

N is chosen by the implementation, kept per context, and need not be the same for every context. For a new stream the compressor sets N and sends N+1 FULL_HEADER packets, and MUST repeat each later COMPRESSED_UDP update N+1 times. The decompressor learns N by counting the repeated FULL_HEADER packets, or from the change in the 4-bit sequence number if some are lost. A miscount can only make it assume a smaller N, which is safe: at worst it sends an unnecessary CONTEXT_STATE.

If a constant field (such as the IP TOS) changes while the N+1 FULL_HEADER packets are being sent, the compressor MUST send N+1 more. To prevent the decompressor from overestimating N, the compressor MUST change the generation number whenever it starts a new run of N+1 FULL_HEADER packets; for IPv4 this is a change from RFC 2508. CONTEXT_STATE packets SHOULD also be repeated N+1 times.
sections.eli5: If you shout a message three times in a row, someone can still catch it even if they miss a couple of shouts. The sender picks how many repeats based on how bumpy the road is.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a stream where an audio codec sends a sample every 10 milliseconds, with a talkspurt of 1 second, 2 seconds of silence, then another talkspurt. Packets are shown as FH (FULL_HEADER), CR (COMPRESSED_RTP) and CU (COMPRESSED_UDP).

In the first case the IPv4 ID does not increment at a constant rate. Plain CRTP handles the lossless case with CR packets, but one lost packet cannot be recovered because the twice algorithm fails on the unpredictable IPv4 ID, so the context must be invalidated. With enhanced CRTP and N=2, three FH packets start the stream, the timestamp and delta are sent in three CU packets, and afterwards the compressor sends only the absolute IPv4 ID, never the delta.

When the delta IP ID is constant, or for IPv6, enhanced CRTP can use the more efficient CR packet once the deltas are established. After the silence gap, the changed timestamp is sent in three CU packets while keeping the deltas, and then CR packets resume.
sections.eli5: The examples show a phone call. Each time the timing changes, such as after a quiet moment, the sender repeats the new timing three times before going back to the short messages.

sections.title: Negotiation
sections.content: Whether CRTP is used on a link is a function of the link-layer protocol, and negotiation is expected to be defined separately for each link layer. Link layers that already negotiate CRTP as in RFC 2508 will need an extension to indicate enhanced CRTP, since the syntax of the existing packet formats has been extended. The reference list includes RFC 3544, IP Header Compression over PPP.
sections.eli5: Both ends of the link must agree to use the new shortcut before they start, because the messages look a bit different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encryption removes the redundancy that header compression exploits, which creates pressure to skip encryption on low-bandwidth links. Where encrypting only the data is acceptable, the Secure RTP work (listed as Work in Progress) leaves headers in the clear so compression can still be applied.

A malfunctioning or malicious compressor could make the decompressor rebuild packets that differ from the originals but still have valid headers and even valid UDP checksums. End-to-end authentication and integrity mechanisms, which compression does not affect, can detect that.

The CONTEXT_STATE packet is not authenticated. An attacker on the link could inject false ones and reduce compression efficiency, probably causing congestion, but such an attacker could disrupt traffic in many other ways. The RFC says this compression has no significant non-uniform decompression load, so the denial-of-service threat from pathological datagrams does not apply in a meaningful way.
sections.eli5: Shortcuts only work on messages you can read, so locking everything makes them useless. Also, nobody checks who sends the "please resend" note, but someone who can tamper with the road could cause worse trouble anyway.
